The multilayer measured averaged transmittance of 82.8% and peak transmittance of 90.3% in the 400-850nm wavelength range (Figure 11) pertinent to PSCs, and exhibited low sheet resistance (4.65 Ω/Sq.). Despite this promising result, the effects of Ag layer morphology on absorption, light scattering, transmittance, and conductivity are still not well understood, and various deposition conditions for a range of Ag film thicknesses must be analyzed to identify the optimal tradeoff between optical and electrical properties. In addition, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) measurements on these samples are required to provide accurate complex refractive indexes to better predict optical behavior in fully integrated multilayer systems. WVTR of TCO/Metal/TCO Inorganic Multilayer Systems on Polymer Substrates – Beyond optical and electrical optimizations, the barrier properties of the multilayer systems must be validated. As concurrent optimization of transparency, electrical conductivity, and WVTR constrains the evaluation of our system, the WVTR optimization 23/52 DE-EE0010241 Nicolas Gaillard was conducted separately from the optical and electrical optimizations. First, a 310 µm thick Aluzine epoxy laminate was used as a substrate to deposit a 60nm-IZO/20nm- Ag/60nm-IZO TMT structure for WVTR testing. Testing was conducted at a 3rd party testing center (Flex Pack Engineering Inc: lead time 1-2 weeks) to circumvent the long lead times at NREL (> 4 months). The 3rd party testing center uses a MOCON testing system, which offers a quick and accurate assessment of WVTR for barrier systems with a detection limit of 0.002 g/m2/day,142 directly facilitating the fast-paced development necessary for this project. Initial assessment of the 60nm-IZO/20nm-Ag/60nm- IZO/310µm-Aluzine sample showed no improvement in WVTR of 2.6 g/m2/day (1.12 g- mm/m2/day) compared to the polymer laminate alone. The consensus on barrier systems suggests that the main avenue of gas transport occurs at defect sites (e.g., pinholes, grain boundaries, low-density films).49,51–53 As such, it is important to reduce the size and number of defects to reduce WVTRs.143 The initial analysis of the sputtered inorganic IZO/Ag/IZO multilayers reflects poor film quality, and the thin films were evaluated to identify critical shortcomings in sample processing. Although improper surface preparation and transport were initially suspected to be the main contributors of seed particles (i.e., dust, residue, contaminants), the plasma-based PVD process itself was noted to be a generator of seed particles due to flaking chamber components and fixtures.144 Surface imaging using the Renishaw microscope system confirmed that the majority of defect sites were a direct result of particle contamination from the sputtering chamber. As shown in Figure 12a, the particles appeared to be significantly thicker than the thin film and exhibited surface striations and sharp edges. As observed in Figure 12b, the particle sample taken from within the chamber using Kapton tape shows a strong correlation in shape and texture to that observed on the sputtered thin film.
